title: Glossopteris flora spreads across Gondwana

facts.text: Glossopteridales, an extinct order of seed plants, are known from the Permian of Gondwana.
Once Gondwana had fused with Pangaea, glossopterid trees, chiefly Glossopteris, dominated large parts of the south.
As glaciation waned in the Middle Permian, the Glossopteris flora flourished and huge coal deposits formed, as in southern Brazil and Uruguay.
These forests collapsed in the end-Permian mass extinction.

title: Gondwanide orogeny

facts.text: Mountain building in the Permian deformed southern Gondwana, in what are now southern South America, South Africa, Antarctica, Australia and New Guinea.
Its folds survive in Argentina's Sierra de la Ventana and South Africa's Cape Fold Belt.
Uplift linked to it split Brazil's Paraná Basin in two.
In South Africa, folding continued into a new phase from about 260 Ma, after the ice sheets had melted and a great lake, the Karoo Sea, spread.

title: Lepidosaur and archelosaur lines split

facts.text: The lineage of lizards and their kin (Lepidosauromorpha) is thought to have split from its sister group, Archelosauria, during the Permian.

title: Pangaea fully assembled

facts.text: During the Permian almost every major landmass was gathered into the supercontinent Pangaea; only parts of East Asia, such as Cathaysia, lay apart.
Gondwana's collision with the northern continents completed the bulk of Pangaea, leaving the Appalachian–Ouachita mountains near its centre.
The consolidated supercontinent stretched from the equator to both polar regions.
Kazakhstania struck Baltica in the Cisuralian and Siberia joined in the late Permian; North China, South China and Indochina fused with Pangaea by the period's end.
Pangaea was complete roughly 20 million years before the end-Permian extinction.

title: Pangean megamonsoon takes hold

facts.text: Permian climate was extremely seasonal, ruled by megamonsoons that brought high aridity and harsh seasons to Pangaea's interior.
Monsoon circulation shows in Permian rocks; Early Permian wind directions record a summer wet season.
As the continents drifted north and spread more evenly across the equator, the megamonsoon intensified.
Dryness alternating with seasonal rain became the normal climate across much of the continent.

facts.text: The Permian begins with the first appearance of the conodont Streptognathodus isolatus.
Its reference section lies in the Aidaralash River valley near Aqtöbe, Kazakhstan.

title: Insects diversify; modern orders appear

facts.text: Insects diversified dramatically in the Early Permian, and most living insect orders arose during the period.
Insects with complete metamorphosis radiated, and scorpionflies, true dragonflies and barklice first appeared.
Older dominant groups, the palaeodictyopterans and giant griffinflies, declined; the palaeodictyopteran decline from the mid-Permian is linked to a change in flora.
Insects and plants were already locked in an arms race of feeding damage and plant defences.

title: Neo-Tethys opens as Cimmeria rifts away

facts.text: Rifting along northern Gondwana broke off the Cimmerian blocks, including Sibumasu (Shan–Thai), Qiantang and Lhasa, in the Early Permian.
The Neo-Tethys Ocean opened behind them as they drifted toward Laurasia, closing the Paleo-Tethys ahead.
A rift in what is now the Himalayan region grew into the Neo-Tethys, an ocean that would dominate much of the Mesozoic.

title: Patagonia collides with Gondwana

facts.text: The Patagonian landmass first touched south-western Gondwana in the mid-Carboniferous; the broader collision came in the early Permian.
Deformation and metamorphism from the collision continued into the Permian.

title: Synapsids dominate the land

facts.text: Pelycosaurs, early synapsids, peaked in the Cisuralian and were the dominant land animals for some 40 million years.
Synapsids, the group that later gave rise to mammals, thrived and diversified greatly, quickly growing large.
Early Permian faunas of North America and Europe were led by plant-eating edaphosaurids and meat-eating sphenacodontids, alongside diadectids and amphibians.
Pelycosaurs and their descendants, the therapsids, are the commonest land vertebrates in the best-known Permian fossil beds.
A few pelycosaurs lingered: the youngest known, from South Africa, is about 260 million years old.

title: Urals rise as Kazakhstania meets Baltica

facts.text: The Kazakhstania block collided with Baltica during the Cisuralian.
The Uralian orogeny built the Ural Mountains during the Permian.
Deformation carried on from the Carboniferous, and granites intruded the region extensively.

title: Carbon dioxide quadruples after a record low

facts.text: Atmospheric CO2 hit a record low about 298 Ma, then rose abruptly fourfold by 294 Ma.
Cooling had limited plant growth and rising oxygen fed more fires; both returned CO2 to the air, reaching about 300 ppm in the Permian.
Rising seas drowned the coal swamps that had buried carbon, so more CO2 stayed in the atmosphere and warmed the planet.
By the Cisuralian, oxygen and carbon dioxide had returned to more normal levels.

verification.title: Rapid rise in atmospheric CO2 marked the end of the Late Palaeozoic Ice Age

facts.text: A large igneous province centred on today's Skagerrak strait erupted at 297 ± 4 Ma.
It covered at least 0.5 million km², including the Oslo and Skagerrak grabens, south-western Sweden, Scotland, northern England and the central North Sea.
It is the oldest of a series of provinces tied to the African superplume, followed by Bachu, Emeishan, the Siberian Traps and the Central Atlantic.
It is tied to the Moscovian and Kasimovian stages of the rainforest collapse, about 310–296 Ma, together with Siberia's Barguzin-Vitim province.

title: Central Pangean Mountains at their peak

facts.text: The range rose where Euramerica collided with northern Gondwana in the Variscan and Alleghanian orogenies, which began about 340 Ma and ended about 295 Ma.
At its highest, in the early Permian, it rivalled today's Himalayas; its western part, the Appalachians, was uplifted then.
Lying along the equator, it cast a rain shadow that turned northern coal swamps into seasonally dry land and later aided Europe's Zechstein salt deposits.
Weathering cut the peaks to about half their height by the Late Permian; its debris spread sandstone and conglomerate across Europe.
Remnants include the Appalachian and Ouachita Mountains, the Atlas and the Bohemian Massif.
The pelycosaur Dimetrodon evolved about 295 Ma.
Pelycosaurs such as Dimetrodon diversified; its remains occur at Bromacker in Germany and in the Red Beds of Texas.

facts.text: The first beetles appeared near the start of the Permian, about 295 Ma.
By the Late Permian there were members of Archostemata, Adephaga and probably Polyphaga, the most diverse group of modern beetles.
Beetles became one of the four great insect radiations.

title: Panjal Traps erupt in northwest India

facts.text: The Panjal Traps, a large igneous province, erupted in what is now northwestern India; zircons give a uranium-lead age of 289 ± 2 Ma.
Their lavas, up to 2,500 m thick in Ladakh and Kashmir, may once have covered over 200,000 square km, comparable to the Emeishan Traps.
They are tied to the opening of the Neo-Tethys Ocean, which carried the Cimmerian blocks away from Gondwana's northeastern margin.
Lava chemistry shifts from enriched continental types to depleted ocean-floor types; the eruptions took place at about 33 degrees south.
Once linked to the Capitanian or end-Permian extinctions, they are far older; the Siberian Traps are the better candidate for those.

verification.title: No link between the Panjal Traps (Kashmir) and the Late Permian mass extinctions

facts.text: When the Permian began, the Late Paleozoic Ice Age was at its peak.
By 287 Ma temperatures had risen and the south polar ice cap retreated in the Artinskian Warming Event; glaciers clung on in eastern Australia's uplands.
Ice sheets shrank from the late Sakmarian on, a deglaciation sometimes treated as the end of the ice age proper.
Around 285.1 Ma orbital cycles stopped driving glacial growth and began driving marine anoxia and aridity, the turning point from icehouse to greenhouse.
As the glaciers receded, sea levels rose and the continental interiors dried out.

facts.text: An impact in Quebec, Canada, formed the 36 km Clearwater West crater 286.2 ± 2.6 Ma, in the Early Permian.
Its neighbour Clearwater East is about 460-470 Ma old; different magnetic and meteorite signatures show that adjacent craters need not be twins.
It is a complex crater whose central peak formed when the crater walls collapsed and the floor rebounded.

facts.text: Subduction-related volcanism along Gondwana's western margin built the Choiyoi province, in today's Argentina and Chile, from about 286 to 247 Ma.
Its lavas, breccias and rhyolitic ignimbrites cover at least 200,000 and probably 500,000 square km, reaching 2-4 km thick.
During the Permian the arc magmatism migrated 350 km inland, reaching San Rafael about 280 Ma.
In Patagonia, Late Permian slab break-off melted the crust, an episode preserved in the Choiyoi volcanic province.
It has been suggested as an additional cause of the end-Permian extinction.

title: Mesosaurs and the earliest amniote embryos

facts.text: The Artinskian Mangrullo Formation of Brazil and Uruguay is rich in mesosaur fossils and holds the earliest known amniote embryos.
Mesosaurus fossils also occur in Permian black shales of Brazil's Paraná Basin, alongside Glossopteris coals.

conflicts.note: Paraná Basin: the Irati Formation, famous for its Mesosaurus fauna, is Late Permian

title: Late Kungurian to early Capitanian cool interval

facts.text: Cooling resumed in the late Kungurian, bringing a cool glacial interval that lasted into the early Capitanian.
Even so, average temperatures stayed much higher than at the start of the Cisuralian; in Australia the P3 glaciation was largely alpine.
Weathering of large igneous provinces emplaced in the Kungurian drew down carbon dioxide and brought on the P3 glaciation.

facts.text: The oldest confirmed bennettitalean fossils, leaves from the Upper Shihhotse Formation of Shanxi, China, date to the early Kungurian, about 281 Ma.
The group became a prominent part of floras only in the Late Triassic, holding that place for much of the Mesozoic.
The oldest bennettitalean reproductive structures, Williamsonia 'flowers', come from the Early Triassic of Australia.

facts.text: An impact in the Early or Middle Permian, about 280 ± 10 Ma, left a buried 11 km crater at Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine.
About 275 Ma the Grand Canyon region dried out and quartz sand dunes spread across a growing desert, forming the Coconino Sandstone.
Deserts seem to have been widespread on Pangaea, and desert dunes and evaporites dominated its interior.
Wind piled its quartz sand into large cross-bedded dunes, famous for trackways of scorpion-like arthropods and early tetrapods.

facts.text: Therapsids, the synapsid line leading to mammals, split from pelycosaur-grade synapsids around 275 Ma.
No confirmed therapsid fossils come from the Early Permian, leaving a long ghost lineage.
Raranimus, from the early Middle Permian of China, is probably the earliest-diverging known therapsid.
Accounts differ on when the major therapsid groups had all appeared: by 275 Ma, or by 265 Ma in the Wordian.

title: Ceratitid ammonoids appear

facts.text: Ceratitid ammonoids arose in the Middle Permian from the daraelitid family of prolecanitids.
Little harmed by the Capitanian extinction, they radiated to dominate Late Permian ammonoids as goniatitids declined.
Ceratitids went on to include almost all Triassic ammonoid genera.

title: Guadalupian reef peak and the Capitan Reef

facts.text: Reef building peaked in the Guadalupian, with reefs abundant from the Delaware Basin and Zechstein Basin to the Tethys and cool Panthalassa shelves.
Texas's Capitan Reef, the best-known example, was built mainly by calcareous sponges and encrusting algae rather than corals.
Brachiopods were key ecosystem engineers in Permian reef complexes.
Later, tectonics restricted the Hovey Channel; rising heat and salinity killed the reef, and brines laid down the Castile Formation evaporites.
The Capitan Formation, a giant fossil reef curving around the Delaware Basin that may have risen 61-91 m above the seafloor, is called the world's best-preserved Paleozoic reef complex.

title: Therapsids take over from pelycosaurs

facts.text: Therapsids replaced pelycosaurs as the dominant large land animals in the Guadalupian, a role they kept into the Early Triassic.
The takeover came as the world grew drier; a poor fossil record across 'Olson's Gap' hides how it unfolded.
Giant dinocephalians, both plant- and meat-eaters, dominated Middle Permian faunas of South Africa and Russia.
Therocephalians arose and took over the sabre-toothed predator niche.
Coastal swamp corridors along East Pangaea let animals migrate between what are now South Africa and Russia.

title: Sea level falls to a Paleozoic low

facts.text: Sea level stood several tens of metres above today's through the Early Permian.
A sharp fall began in the Roadian, reaching the lowest level of the whole Paleozoic, near today's, in the Wuchiapingian.
This Permian regression may be tied to the formation of Pangaea.
Falling seas, rising carbon dioxide and a worsening climate marked the Lopingian, ending in the end-Permian extinction.

title: Olson's Extinction

facts.text: A proposed extinction around 273 Ma, in the late Cisuralian or early Guadalupian, long before the end-Permian crisis.
Most pelycosaur lineages vanished: edaphosaurids and ophiacodontids died out near the Kungurian–Roadian boundary while caseids and therapsids diversified.
Temnospondyl amphibians declined sharply afterwards, and extinction rates in fish rose.
Extreme environments in Kansas, combining heat and acidic waters, coincide with it, pointing to climate change as a possible cause.
A review of Kungurian and Roadian beds found the faunal turnover real, not a shift in where fossils were sampled.

contested_note: Some authors argue the extinction is an artefact of poor sampling or gradual change, and the timing of 'Olson's Gap' is contested.

facts.text: Sabre-toothed gorgonopsians first evolved about 270 Ma and lasted until about 252 Ma.
The oldest identifiable one, Phorcys, dates to about the Wordian–Capitanian boundary, but finds show the group was diversifying by the early Wordian.
Small at first, with 10–15 cm skulls, they grew to bear-like sizes; Inostrancevia reached 3.5 m and about 300 kg.
Once the Capitanian extinction removed the dinocephalians, gorgonopsians became apex predators.

facts.text: Arc accretion in the Permian and Triassic affected about 2,500 km of eastern Australia's continental margin.
Major contraction came about 270–260 Ma and around 253 Ma, with a later phase about 235–230 Ma; a megafold had formed earlier, around 290 Ma.
Pangaea's counterclockwise rotation drove transpression along the subduction zone of the eastern Australian margin.
Its foredeep, the Sydney–Bowen basins, filled with sediment that built vast coal deposits.

title: Capitanian carbon-isotope rise and cooling

facts.text: Marine limestones of Capitanian age record a rise in carbon-13, reflecting a cooling of global climate.
This cooling may have caused the end-Capitanian extinction of warm-water species such as large fusulinids, alatoconchid bivalves and waagenophyllid rugose corals.

title: Capitanian mass extinction

facts.text: It began around 262 Ma and peaked around 259 Ma, closing the Capitanian stage and the Guadalupian (Middle Permian) epoch.
About 33–35% of marine genera and 60–63% of marine species died out; ammonoids, corals, reef algae, foraminifera, bryozoans and brachiopods suffered most.
On land the dinocephalians and the last varanopids vanished, and anomodont diversity halved.
It is linked to the Emeishan eruptions, which drove two ocean anoxic events and acidification, and to a sea-level fall that killed reefs.
Its severity is debated: some rank it fifth worst ecologically, while others find only low-latitude northern taxa hit, or a regional South China crisis.

contested_note: How severe and how global it was is still debated; some studies see only a regional crisis or a gradual decline.

facts.text: Eruptions of this flood-basalt province in south-western China began 265 Ma or earlier, peaked between 262 and 261 Ma, and ended about 259 Ma.
The basalts cover more than 250,000 km², up to 5.5 km thick, with an estimated volume of about 300,000 km³.
The eruptions had global ecological impact and are tied to the Capitanian mass extinction, though they were dwarfed by the later Siberian Traps.
Around 260 Ma the Emeishan Thermal Excursion interrupted a mid-Capitanian cool period; afterwards weathering of the basalts drew down CO2 and cooled the early Wuchiapingian.
Coronene enrichment at the Guadalupian–Lopingian boundary, without an iridium anomaly, points to massive volcanism rather than an impact.

facts.text: Cynodonts, the therapsid group ancestral to mammals, first appeared in the Late Permian, about 260 Ma, and spread worldwide.
The earliest known cynodont, Charassognathus, comes from the Wuchiapingian; they are the only major therapsid group with no Middle Permian record.
They diversified rapidly after the end-Permian extinction.

title: End-Guadalupian sea-level fall and reef crisis

facts.text: The Guadalupian–Lopingian boundary, dated by ash beds to 259.857 ± 0.084 Ma, coincided with one of the Phanerozoic's most prominent marine regressions.
Evaporites and land deposits lie over marine carbonates across the boundary, and a vast unconformity marks it in strata worldwide.
Falling seas and regional salinity swings ended the golden age of reef building in the 'end-Guadalupian reef crisis'.
Closure of the Sino-Mongolian Seaway has been proposed as a driver of biodiversity loss in the Paleo-Tethys.
Global diversity, rebuilt by disaster taxa late in the Guadalupian, dropped again in the Wuchiapingian.

facts.text: Callistophytales, seed ferns whose coal forests had covered South China, make their last appearance in the Wuchiapingian.

title: Dicynodonts and pareiasaurs flourish

facts.text: Late Permian lands were dominated by advanced therapsids, sabre-toothed gorgonopsians and beaked plant-eating dicynodonts, alongside large herbivorous pareiasaurs.
Dicynodonts flourished after the Capitanian extinction and became among the most successful therapsids, surviving almost to the end of the Triassic.
South Africa's Beaufort Group was then a semi-arid cold steppe, crossed by seasonal rivers draining into the Karoo Sea.

title: First archosauromorph reptiles

facts.text: Archosauromorphs, the reptiles that later produced pseudosuchians, dinosaurs and pterosaurs, first appeared and diversified in the Late Permian.
The first archosauriforms appeared in the latest Permian.
A molecular estimate puts the split of turtles from the line of birds and crocodilians at about 255 Ma.
A marine clade of ichthyosauromorphs, sauropterygians and thalattosaurs may have originated from archosauromorphs in the Late Permian.
Archosauromorphs exploded in diversity after the end-Permian extinction.

title: First gliding vertebrates

facts.text: Weigeltisaurids, lizard-like reptiles with extendable wings like modern gliding lizards, are the oldest known gliding vertebrates.
Their worldwide spread shows that tall, thin forests had become widespread by the Late Permian.

facts.text: From the latest Permian a broad zone of lithospheric stretching formed across Pangaea along the line of the future Central Atlantic.
Extension that began in the late Permian spread across Laurussia from central Europe to eastern Canada, opening north–south rift valleys.
Pangaea's breakup can loosely be traced back to about 252 Ma.

title: Kupferschiefer anoxia in the early Zechstein Sea

facts.text: About 257 Ma, anoxic water in the enclosed Zechstein basin laid down the Kupferschiefer, a black shale and marl at the base of the Zechstein Group.
Though usually only 30-60 cm thick, it spreads over 600,000 square km across six countries and holds up to 30% organic matter.
Mineral-rich groundwater later formed sulfide ores in it, one of the world's most important copper deposits, mined since at least 1199 AD.

title: Zechstein Sea lays down thick salt

facts.text: A marine transgression, probably tied to deglaciation, created the Zechstein Sea, a hypersaline inland sea over today's North Sea, lowland Britain, Germany and Poland.
In the rain shadow of the Central Pangean Mountains near the equator, at least five evaporation cycles piled up salt, anhydrite and dolomite about 1,000 m thick.
The sea's eventual disappearance was part of the marine regression that preceded and accompanied the end-Permian extinction.

title: End of the Late Paleozoic icehouse

facts.text: The Late Paleozoic icehouse, under way since the Late Devonian, finally ended around 255 Ma.
It was the most extensive and longest icehouse of the Phanerozoic.
A last regional glaciation, P4, lasted in Australia from the middle Capitanian to the late Wuchiapingian.
The final alpine glaciers melted in what is now eastern Australia around 255 Ma, in the late Wuchiapingian.
By one account, the last greenhouse period began in the late Permian as this ice age ended.

facts.text: An impact left a 40 km crater on the border of Mato Grosso and Goiás, Brazil, where there was probably a shallow sea.
Its age, 254.7 ± 2.5 Ma, overlaps the Permian–Triassic boundary, and some suggest the warming it caused helped trigger the extinction.

title: Castile evaporites fill the Delaware Basin

facts.text: As tectonics restricted the Hovey Channel, the deep Delaware Basin of Texas and New Mexico was cut off from the sea and its brines grew ever saltier.
Up to 91 m of finely laminated gypsum and anhydrite, the Castile Formation, settled in water over 500 m deep, followed by thick halite of the Salado.
By the end of the Ochoan the basin had filled to the top of the Capitan Reef and was mostly dry land.

facts.text: Basalt lava flooded a vast area of Siberia; about 7 million km2 of basalt, some 4 million km3, remains today.
It was one of the largest volcanic events of the last 500 million years, erupting for roughly two million years across the Permian–Triassic boundary.
Magma heated the coal- and evaporite-rich rocks of the Tungus basin, which can release large amounts of toxic and greenhouse gases.
Its CO2, SO2, halogens and metals drove warming, ocean anoxia and acidification, ozone loss, acid rain and repeated mercury poisoning.
Zircon dating ties the eruptions to the extinction, and the traps are believed to be its primary cause.

facts.text: Glossopteris trees dominated much of southern Gondwana through the Permian, until these ecosystems collapsed in the end-Permian extinction.
In Australia the flora collapsed around 370,000 years before the boundary; in western Gondwana probably a few hundred thousand years before.
Just above the boundary, an Australia-wide conifer flora largely replaced it.
The glossopterid order arose at the start of the Permian; most or all of its members died out in the extinction, 251.9 million years ago.
A large, abrupt global fall in δ13C coincides with the extinction and helps locate the boundary in rocks that cannot be dated radiometrically.
The negative excursion measured 4–7% and lasted about 500,000 years, though alteration of the rocks makes its exact size hard to pin down.
Carbonate rocks worldwide record a swift drop of about 1% in the 13C/12C ratio.
Methane from clathrates was once favoured as the light-carbon source, but isotopes point mainly to volcanic CO2 and thermogenic methane from the Siberian Traps.
A burst of methane-producing microbes may explain part of the swings; on land, Norwegian floras turned over before the big negative shift.
The Siberian Traps released more than 5 teratonnes of CO2, more than doubling the atmosphere's carbon dioxide.
CO2 rose from around 400 to 2,500 ppm as some 3,900–12,000 gigatonnes of carbon entered the ocean-atmosphere system.
Average surface temperature jumped from about 18 °C to as much as 35 °C; tropical seas off Iran topped 35 °C.
This rapid greenhouse release caused the extinction and began an extreme hothouse lasting several million years into the Triassic.
Earth's most severe known extinction, it removed about 57% of families, 62% of genera, 81% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrate species.
The main marine pulse took 60,000–100,000 years; U–Pb dating of Meishan ash beds places it between 251.941 and 251.880 Ma.
The consensus cause is the Siberian Traps eruptions, whose CO2 and SO2 brought global warming, sulfurous oxygen-starved seas and acidified oceans.
Shell-building marine animals suffered most; on land it was the largest insect mass extinction and equally catastrophic for plants.
It ended the Paleozoic Era; recovery was slow, with land ecosystems needing some 30 million years to rebuild.

title: End-Permian ocean acidification and acid rain

facts.text: Rising CO2 acidified the oceans, by up to 0.7 pH units, matching the selective loss of heavily calcified animals.
Acidification was worst at mid-latitudes; with anoxia, a marine transgression devastated shallow shelf communities.
On land, acid rain lowered soil pH and sped soil erosion, washing land-derived organic matter into the sea.
Oxygen-starved and hydrogen-sulfide-rich (euxinic) waters spread through the oceans from the Late Permian into the Early Triassic.
Across most of the Tethys and Panthalassa, anoxia appears at the extinction itself, though at some sites it began earlier.
Sulfate-reducing bacteria thrived and filled the sea with hydrogen sulfide, even in the sunlit shallows.
Hydrogen sulfide escaping from the sea may have poisoned life on land and in the water.
The extinction, triggered by runaway Siberian Traps CO2, was marked by ocean deoxygenation; ocean overturn has also been proposed.

facts.text: Global sea level is reported to have fallen 250 m during the Permian–Triassic extinction.
A drastic regression shrank shallow shelf habitats, hastening the final decline of trilobites.
Other work ties the main warming to a marine transgression, which with anoxia ravaged shallow shelf life.
The acanthodians or 'spiny sharks', an early class of jawed fishes, became extinct in the Permian–Triassic extinction.
Their diversity had been low but stable through the Carboniferous and slipped further in the Permian.
Fusulinid foraminifera, large single-celled shell-builders, went extinct in the Permian–Triassic extinction.
The Capitanian crisis had already cut them to dwarf forms, and they were nearly gone before the final blow.
Lagenid forams survived, probably thanks to wider environmental tolerance and range.
Sabre-toothed gorgonopsians, the Late Permian's top land predators, died out in the extinction's final phase.
They began to disappear from Africa and Eastern Europe just before the extinction.
Biarmosuchians also vanished, while dicynodonts, therocephalians and cynodonts shrank to a handful of species each.
Several Paleozoic insect groups, including the giant griffinflies (protodonates) and palaeodictyopteroids, were extinct by the end of the Permian.
Of the Paleozoic insect groups, only three are known after the extinction, the largest known mass extinction of insects.
The Noeggerathiales, the last surviving progymnosperms, persisted until the end of the Permian.
Progymnosperms were woody, spore-bearing plants thought to have given rise to the seed plants.
Rugose and tabulate corals, the reef-building corals of the Paleozoic, died out in the Permian–Triassic extinction.
About 96% of coral and other anthozoan genera were lost.

title: Last tree lycopsid swamps in Cathaysia

facts.text: Carboniferous-style lycopod and horsetail swamps survived to the end of the Permian only in Cathaysia, equatorial islands that became South China.
By then tree lycopsids were rare, marginal plants there, no longer the main coal formers.
Trilobites, which had thrived since the Cambrian, vanished at the end of the Permian after nearly 300 million years.
The Proetida, the only order left after the Devonian, lasted to the end; by the Changhsingian a handful of genera remained, by one count just two.
Falling sea level shrank their shallow-shelf habitats, so their final decline came shortly before the main extinction.
Near the end of the Permian, Pangaea grew drier as the supercontinent coalesced.
Terminal Permian volcanism and global warming sharply worsened this aridity.
In the Kuznetsk Basin of Siberia, drying killed humid-adapted Cordaites forests a few hundred thousand years before the boundary.

title: Proposed end-Permian impact (largely rejected)

facts.text: Suggestions that an asteroid impact triggered the extinction are now largely rejected.
Candidate craters include the 250 km Bedout structure off northwest Australia and a hypothesized 480 km Wilkes Land crater in Antarctica.
Reported clues include shocked quartz, fullerenes with extraterrestrial gases and meteorite fragments, but iridium is not anomalous and many boundary sites lack impact evidence.

contested_note: An impact trigger is largely rejected; the proposed craters are all contentious and their ages and origins still debated.

title: Last eurypterids (sea scorpions)

facts.text: Eurypterids, the 'sea scorpions', dwindled in numbers and diversity through the Permian.
When they died out is contentious: either early in the Middle Permian or in the Permian–Triassic extinction, 251.9 million years ago.
A terminal-Permian cuticle fragment from Australia, once called the youngest eurypterid, may instead be a scorpion.

contested_note: The timing of their extinction is contentious: early Middle Permian or the end-Permian extinction.
